title: Boerner & Schulz (2009) True/False Quiz
instructions: Choose True if the statement agrees with the article and False otherwise. Diagnostic criteria discussed here are proposals described in the 2009 paper, not current diagnostic guidance. Keep risk associations, possible explanations, and findings from cited studies distinct.

items.prompt: The cumulative stress perspective proposes that caregiving stress and the death together deplete coping resources.
items.explanation: The wear-and-tear hypothesis predicts that the combined stresses contribute to greater adjustment difficulties after the loss. It is one perspective on caregivers' experiences, not a universal outcome.
items.source: Three perspectives on caregiving and bereavement

items.prompt: According to the stress reduction perspective, a person who feels relief after the death does not experience grief.
items.explanation: Relief may arise when caregiving strain and a loved one's suffering end. The authors do not equate relief with an absence of grief or affection; different responses can coexist.

items.prompt: The authors suggest that depletion, relief, and anticipation can coexist within the same caregiver's experience.
items.explanation: A caregiver may be exhausted, relieved that suffering has ended, and partly prepared for the death and life afterward. The perspectives may combine, with different patterns across caregivers.

items.prompt: The 2009 review reports that a minority of bereaved caregivers, approximately 10–20%, continued to experience high stress and psychiatric problems after the death.
items.explanation: The authors contrast the generally positive prognosis described for many caregivers with persistent difficulties in a substantial minority. This estimate summarizes the literature they cited, rather than a universal rate for every caregiver population.

items.prompt: The reported figure of 30% at risk for clinical depression in the dementia-caregiver study refers to one year after the death.
items.explanation: The authors report that 30% of caregivers in their cited dementia-caregiver research were at risk for clinical depression one year post-death. Being at risk is not the same as a confirmed diagnosis in every person counted.

items.prompt: The proposed complicated-grief criteria described in the 2009 article required two of eight additional symptoms alongside persistent yearning.
items.explanation: The historical proposal required four of the eight symptoms, occurring several times a day and/or causing severe distress, alongside persistent disruptive yearning. These are the criteria summarized in the 2009 paper, not a statement of current diagnostic requirements.
items.source: Complicated-grief criteria proposed at the time

items.prompt: Under the diagnostic proposal described in this 2009 article, symptoms lasting only three months satisfied the duration requirement.
items.explanation: The proposal required distressing symptoms to last at least six months and significantly impair functioning in important areas of life. This refers specifically to the historical criteria presented in the article.

items.prompt: The 2009 article treats complicated grief as distinct from depression and PTSD while acknowledging that they can co-occur.
items.explanation: In discussing the diagnostic concept and proposals current at that time, the authors describe co-occurrence but argue that complicated grief requires distinct treatment strategies. This is the article's historical account.
items.source: Co-occurrence and diagnostic distinction in the article

items.prompt: Reporting a very positive caregiving experience always lowers the risk of complicated grief.
items.explanation: Some caregivers with complicated grief also reported positive caregiving experiences. The authors suggest that losing a central role, source of meaning, or close relationship may help explain this pattern; they do not establish that positive caregiving itself causes grief difficulties.
items.source: Positive caregiving and vulnerability after loss

items.prompt: Being prepared informationally and pragmatically was taken to mean that the caregiver was equally prepared emotionally.
items.explanation: The cited focus-group study proposed emotional, pragmatic, and informational components of preparedness. Participants could feel prepared in the latter two areas while still feeling entirely unprepared emotionally.

items.prompt: A relatively certain death and a long period of caregiving do not guarantee that the caregiver feels prepared.
items.explanation: The reviewed research included caregivers who felt unprepared despite years of intensive care. Expecting the death is therefore different from feeling prepared for it and for life afterward.

items.prompt: The authors suggest that conversations about caregiving experiences may be helpful both before and after the death.
items.explanation: They propose discussing burden, available support, emotions, positive aspects, and the impact of caregiving on the person's life. The recommendation applies on both sides of the loss.

items.prompt: The article recommends assessing only the negative aspects of caregiving when identifying people at risk of bereavement difficulties.
items.explanation: The authors advise considering positive as well as stressful experiences. A highly valued caregiving role or central relationship may leave a major loss of meaning, so an entirely positive account does not rule out later difficulty.

items.prompt: In the randomized trial cited by the authors, an intervention designed to reduce dementia caregivers' burden and distress before the death had an additional preventive benefit for complicated grief afterward.
items.explanation: The 2009 article reports this additional bereavement benefit from the cited psychosocial-behavioral intervention trial. The claim is specific to that study and does not mean every intervention or every participant had the same outcome.

items.prompt: The article reports that loss-focused cognitive-behavioral techniques and standard interpersonal therapy produced improvement at the same speed in the cited treatment study.
items.explanation: The authors summarize Shear and colleagues' study as finding higher and faster rates of improvement with the loss-focused approach than with standard interpersonal therapy. This comparison describes the cited study, not a universal ranking of current treatments.
